bible_refs.note: Always bearing about in the body the dying of Jesus, that the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our body.
τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τέθεικεν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων
τὴν νέκρωσιν ... περιφέρουσιν ... ἵνα καὶ ἡ ζωὴ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ... φανερωθῇ
The transformation of the body of humiliation to conformity with the body of glory echoes Philippians 3:20-21
The subjection of all things to Christ parallels 1 Corinthians 15:25, 27

choices.why: Infinitive absolute following the participial sense of the prior clause, indicating the state resulting from their action; not a finite verb but the condition affirmed.
Chosen over 'killing' or 'death' because it refers to the ongoing subduing of sin's power in the flesh, not the act of dying itself, consistent with Pauline usage in 2 Corinthians 4:10.
Aorist passive subjunctive indicating a potential outcome of bearing Christ's dying; not 'be shown' (too weak) or 'appear' (intransitive), but specifically 'be made evident' through our mortal frame.
preposition indicating substitution or benefit, standard in sacrificial contexts
theological term for atoning sacrifice, fits context of faith and sin
present middle indicative of διαλογίζομαι, indicates active consideration
The compound ὑπερ- (over) + κόσμος (world) conveys transcendence beyond the created order; 'heavenly' captures the theological sense better than literal 'super-worldly'.
Future active indicative matches the eschatological context; 'transform' is standard for μετασχηματίζω in Pauline-like usage (cf. Phil 3:21), stronger than 'change' or 'alter'.
In Christological contexts (Phil 2:8), ταπείνωσις denotes the voluntary lowering of the divine status; 'humiliation' preserves the theological weight better than 'lowliness' or 'abasement'.

While ἐνέργεια can mean 'energy' or 'activity', in the phrase κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ δύνασθαι it refers to the active exercise of divine might; 'power' is idiomatic in English theological rendering here.
Aorist infinitive expressing purpose; 'subject' is the precise theological term for divine subduing of all powers (cf. 1 Cor 15:25, 27), stronger than 'bring under' or 'subdue'.
Despotēs implies mastery and authority; in religious contexts it translates 'lord' (not 'despot' which is pejorative in English), fitting the imitation of Christ as master.
Aorist subjunctive with ἵνα expresses purpose; 'gain' conveys the active acquisition of life through faith better than 'win' or 'obtain' in this soteriological context.

pass_b_english: They are reckoned as having died, and their going forth was counted as evil treatment; our departure from them is utter destruction. But they are in peace, and their hope of immortality is full. What, then, is the meaning of their labors? Paul again interprets, saying: We always carry about in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus too may be made evident in our mortal flesh.

We affirm there are two ways of understanding this mortification spoken of here: one is intellectual and spiritual, the other is apprehended through bodily sensation. For God, who exists and has come forth from God according to nature, his Only-begotten Word, prepared for himself a body from the earth; he took upon himself this mortal, human frame, endowed with a rational soul. His purpose was to mortify sin in the flesh and to still the impulse of its innate movements that draw us toward outward pleasures.

Yet the Word, being God, did not establish this for his own sake, but that he might see and endure the sufferings beyond those within us. Indeed, he knows no sin. Rather, he has transmuted within himself the entirety of human nature into a holy and blameless life, when he became man and appeared in the form that is with us. Thus he came to hold first place in all things, so that we, following in his steps, might possess within ourselves his mortification — that is, the powerlessness of sin's strength in our flesh — and thereby be empowered to embrace both this mortification and the blameless life into eternal being.

He became obedient to God and Father, as Scripture says, even to the point of death, laying down his life for the sheep. He died once for sin—meaning for the sin of the world—having made propitiation through faith. The one who lives, lives to God. Therefore, the mystagogues carry in their own bodies this mortification, earned through sufferings and continuing even to his death, so that the life of Jesus, as he himself declared, may be revealed in our bodies.

They too shall live to God, living the holy, blameless, and blessed life. He especially remembers this mortification and yet life, for even now the minds of those who came before, tested by trials and hardships which they willingly endured to fulfill the apostles’ glorious course, bear witness. Nor does he in any way less urge us to think thus, solely and interpreting to them what he said.

For he immediately adds: We who live are continually delivered to death through Jesus, so that through these things he shows they willingly endure the death of the flesh, out of piety toward Christ. Their aim is not to gaze upon present things, but to anticipate the future and the rewards of the 347 labors. They make no account of those who sweat from the struggles, but rather seek the heavenly goods, reasoning about the breadth of God’s ambition. Therefore they are delivered to death through Jesus so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in mortal flesh.
What is the life of Jesus? It is incorruptibility and sanctification, great glory and heavenly in nature.

For it will be revealed to us in due seasons when the judge descends from heaven above, and he will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working of his power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.
Thus the death is at work in us, but the life is in you.
